title: Maitreyi's question
hookLine: a husband offers to split the property; his wife asks for something else
carry: hear it, question it, live in it
tomorrow: The man on the lane in Kashi

lines: LET ME DIVIDE WHAT I HAVE.
TELL ME WHAT YOU KNOW INSTEAD.
cards: The sage Yajnavalkya, the one who said neti neti, decides to leave home and live as a wandering monk. He has two wives, and he calls one of them, Maitreyi, to settle things.
Let me divide what I have between you and Katyayani, he says. It's a fair, sensible offer. Maitreyi asks one question.
If this whole earth, full of wealth, were mine, would it make me immortal? No, he says. Your life would be like the life of the rich.
That's all. And she says: then what would I do with something that won't make me immortal? Tell me what you know instead.

teach.b: Yajnavalkya is delighted, and he teaches her. In that conversation in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, he gives a line that became the backbone of the jnana path. Paraphrased: the self is what should be seen.
It should be heard about, reflected on, and deeply meditated on.
Much later, the teacher Shankara and those who followed him made those verbs a method, three steps still taught in Vedanta schools, and the reason Hindu teachers often welcome a student's questions.
First, shravana: hearing. You listen to the teaching, from the Upanishads and from a teacher, carefully, the way Maitreyi listened. Not skimming.
Second, manana: reflecting. You argue with what you've heard and raise every doubt. Does this make sense?
What about this objection? Shankara didn't want blind belief; he spent pages answering objections.
Third, nididhyasana: deep, sustained meditation. Once the doubts have settled, you dwell on the teaching until it's no longer an idea you hold but the way you see.

teach.h: HEAR IT, QUESTION IT, LIVE IN IT.
teach.b: Hear it, test it, soak in it. Shankara also insisted on a teacher. Not a guru to worship blindly, but someone who has walked the road and can point, like the traveler who turned the leader around.
And notice where this began. Not with a debate. With a woman who turned down her share of a fortune and asked for the truth.

how: In Advaita Vedanta, students traditionally study the Upanishads and Shankara's commentaries with a teacher (shravana), work through doubts and questions (manana), and then practice sustained contemplation (nididhyasana).

o: winning a debate by memorizing the most verses
knowing the self by hearing, testing and dwelling on the truth
accepting a teacher's words without asking any questions

games.q: Shankara's three steps — tap the pairs.
p: asked for the truth, not wealth

s: Shankara taught that students should accept the teaching without questions
manana, reflection, means raising every doubt; Shankara answered objections at length.
the three steps come from a line in the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad
Yajnavalkya tells Maitreyi the self is to be heard, reflected on and meditated on.
Maitreyi accepted her share of the property
she asked what she'd do with wealth that couldn't make her immortal, and asked for his knowledge.

games.q: you're Maitreyi. your husband is leaving to be a monk and offers you half his property. what does the Upanishad say you ask?
o: would the whole earth's wealth make me immortal?
games.why: she asks if wealth could make her immortal. told no, she asks for what he knows instead.

practice: Take one small line, I am aware, and first just hear it, letting the words land. Then reflect: is it true right now, is there awareness here? Raise any doubt you honestly have.
If it holds, soak in it: don't repeat the words, just rest in what they point to, the plain fact of being aware.

wordCard.voice: Jnana yoga, Shankara's method: shravana, manana, nididhyasana. Hearing the teaching, reflecting on it, and meditating on it until it becomes how you see.

orig.note: Sanskrit: hearing, reflecting, deep meditation — the three steps of Vedanta study.

carryVoice: Your line: hear it, question it, live in it. On this road, even your doubts get a step of their own. See you next time.

sources.ref: Brihadaranyaka Upanishad 2.4.1–5 (Yajnavalkya and Maitreyi; the self to be seen, heard, reflected on, meditated on)
Shankara, commentary on the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad and Brahma Sutras (the method of shravana, manana, nididhyasana)
